summary:
Alabama is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework carried at the country level.

Facility access is the most immediate state-level exposure. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records Alabama as enacting bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2022 and 2024. House Bill 322, signed 8 April 2022 as Act No. 2022-290 and codified by the Alabama Board of Education in September 2022, requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with the gender recorded on their birth certificate. A March 2024 bill would extend that restriction to university bathrooms, and the July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map records Alabama's "Don't Say Gay" bill as carrying a bathroom ban extending to college campuses. Senate Bill 79, signed February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and allows separate single-sex spaces wherever biology, privacy, safety or fairness are implicated.

Gender-affirming care is a criminal matter for providers. Since 8 May 2022 the Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act (SB 184), signed 8 April 2022, has made it a Class C felony punishable by 10 years in prison for a medical provider to give puberty blockers, hormones or surgery to anyone under age 19. The Eleventh Circuit allowed enforcement from 21 August 2023, and the ban has remained in force since plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025. A trans visitor travelling with a minor dependent has no lawful route to that care from Alabama providers.

Identity documents carry a surgical precondition. Alabama permits amendment of birth certificates and driver's licences to a person's current sex only with documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" together with a name change. A January 2021 federal ruling in Corbitt v. Taylor invalidated the surgery requirement; the Eleventh Circuit reversed, and on 20 September 2024 ruled that refusal to issue accurate licences did not violate the federal constitution, with rehearing denied 13 November 2024 and judgment entered 10 December 2024. The ACLU states that most transgender people therefore cannot obtain an accurate licence and must carry daily identification showing the wrong gender, exposing them to harassment and violence at identity checks.

Sport is restricted by statute at both school levels. House Bill 391, enacted April 2021 with a House vote of 74-19 and signed by Governor Kay Ivey, requires all K-12 athletes to compete on teams of the gender listed on their birth certificate and has applied since 1 July 2021. House Bill 261, signed 30 May 2023, prohibits college and university competition on a team differing from sex assigned at birth even after gender-affirming hormone therapy, except in co-ed sports.

State protection machinery does not reach gender identity. No statewide law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or student harassment and bullying, so a trans visitor refused service has no state public-accommodations recourse. Alabama's hate-crime law, in force since 1994, covers race, colour, religion, national origin, ethnicity and physical or mental disability only and does not apply to crimes based on gender identity.

Marriage recording is statewide. Eight Alabama counties still refused all marriage licences by 2017, until the Legislature in May 2019 required recording of marriage certificates; all counties began recording for all couples including same-sex couples on 29 August 2019, leaving 1996 Executive Order Number 24, Alabama Code section 30-1-19 (1998) and the June 2006 constitutional Amendment 774 unenforceable. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex can have the marriage recorded in every county.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, a category it assigns on the strength of the state's education and facility statutes rather than on any documented incident.

Statewide polling conducted in 2025 places Alabama among the lowest-support states for transgender-inclusive nondiscrimination and access policies; the source reports the ranking only, without the underlying measure or margin.

The legislature has repeatedly declined to broaden its bias-motivated violence statute: a 2009 bill adding sexual orientation passed the House 46-41 on 23 April 2009 but received no full Senate vote before adjournment on 15 May 2009, and further bills in 2016 and 2017 failed. Gender identity has never been added.

Alabama sits in a federal circuit whose appellate rulings have twice shaped the state's document rules, first invalidating and then restoring the surgical precondition, so the operative requirement for a visitor's identification is set by that court rather than by the Alabama legislature alone.
localsOnly:
Discrimination protection exists only at municipal level. Birmingham has prohibited discrimination on these grounds since September 2017 and Montevallo since April 2018, while Huntsville, Tuscaloosa and Montgomery provide public-employment protections only. Residents outside those cities have no local ordinance to rely on.

State law places no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare and provides no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees.

Adoption by same-sex couples is permitted, but the Supreme Court of Alabama held in 2002 that homosexual conduct created a strong presumption of parental unfitness as "abhorrent, immoral, detestable," and the Child Placing Agency Inclusion Act signed by Governor Kay Ivey in May 2017 protects faith-based agencies that refuse placements on religious grounds.

Gender identity has been read into sex under Title VII for employment in Eleventh Circuit jurisdiction since 2011, giving residents a federal employment claim even in the absence of state law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2024 university bathroom bill was enacted is not stated by the source, and the July 2026 assessment's reference to a college-campus bathroom ban is not tied to a bill number; the current scope of the campus restriction is unresolved here.

No Alabama-specific incident data on violence against transgender people, and no documented case of a trans traveller being stopped under the facility or sports statutes, appears in the sourced material. Enforcement practice behind the statutes is not sourced.

Whether Senate Bill 79's single-sex space provision has been challenged in court, and how courts have treated it alongside the facility statutes, is not sourced.

The 2025 polling result is reported only as a relative ranking among states; the population surveyed, the exact question and the period covered are not given.

Whether the surgical precondition for a licence affects entry or identity screening for a visitor entering Alabama is not addressed by any source here.
